title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
gist: Two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, claiming top benchmark scores and big cybersecurity gains, but is withholding broad release pending the US government's voluntary testing framework. Ars notes frontier models cluster within a few points on benchmarks and Carbon may just be a post-trained Argon.

insights.claim: Google is holding back Gemini 4 Carbon under a staged, deliberative release because of its agentic coding and cybersecurity strength, working within the US government's voluntary testing framework before rolling it out via its Fairwinds cyber defense program.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Government pre-release testing is becoming a de facto gate on frontier model launches.
insights.quote: The company is working within the voluntary testing framework established by the US government, and it plans to roll the model out through its Fairwinds cyber defense program once that’s done.

insights.claim: The author predicts Carbon could reach wide availability in a couple of weeks if it follows Argon's pattern, likely first for AI Ultra subscribers and Gemini API developers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Gating periods look short, so the 'can't use it' framing is partly marketing.
insights.quote: if it’s anything like Argon, the model could be available in a couple of weeks

insights.claim: Ars frames Google's 'too capable to release' messaging as a repeating pattern in frontier model announcements.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Capability-withholding claims are now a standard launch narrative, worth discounting.
insights.quote: It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.
insights.locator: Stop me if you’ve heard this

insights.claim: Carbon beats Argon by slim margins on every test and beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 in almost every test, but the gap to competitors is just a few points.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Frontier capability is commoditizing at the top; differentiation shifts elsewhere.
insights.quote: The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
insights.locator: Google has some numbers to support

insights.claim: Ars suggests Carbon, positioned as a new model, may simply be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Rapid 'new model' cadence may reflect post-training iterations rather than new pretraining runs.
insights.quote: Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
insights.locator: Google has some numbers to support

insights.claim: Google says Carbon raised its WebDev Arena score by 89 points to rank fourth on the leaderboard.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Even Google's flagship is not #1 on a key coding leaderboard.
insights.quote: Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena, now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.

insights.claim: Google claims Carbon is twice as likely as Argon to generate vulnerability-free code, and the Chrome team says it is 10 times better at generating high-quality patches than non-Google models.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: AI-driven vulnerability remediation is becoming a headline competitive axis.
insights.quote: Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.

insights.claim: In the Grey Swan prompt-injection evaluation, Carbon had a 0 percent attack success rate versus 0.7 percent for Argon, 1 percent for Opus 5.5 and 8.5 percent for GPT-6 Astra.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Prompt-injection robustness matters for enterprise agent deployment and differentiates vendors more than raw benchmarks.
insights.quote: That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).

insights.claim: Google will offer Carbon at a discounted $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, which will double after an introductory period whose end date Google declined to specify.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Real Carbon pricing is likely $4/$20 per million tokens; current rates are a share-grab subsidy.
insights.quote: Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. That price will double once the introductory period expires.

insights.claim: Argon's discounted rates run only through the end of November, and Google's refusal to give a Carbon end date suggests it hasn't decided when to raise prices.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Pricing flexibility signals Google is competing on price to win API share.
insights.quote: Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
